text: Capacity planning fails most often for a boring reason: someone estimates next quarter's load from memory, or by rounding up last quarter's peak, instead of pulling the real history. Every system with actual traffic already has the raw material for a forecast sitting in its monitoring stack. Getting that forecast right starts with one discipline — go get the real numbers before you touch a spreadsheet.

The workflow is consistent regardless of the system: pull six to twelve months of real request rate, CPU, memory, and storage history from Prometheus, Datadog, or your cloud provider's own metrics. Fit the growth model that actually matches the shape of that curve. Add a confidence band around the trend line, because no forecast projected forward is exact. Then add headroom and provisioning lead time, and re-run the whole thing on a fixed cadence so it never goes stale.

The model you fit matters more than people expect. Plot month-over-month change two ways: is the absolute increment roughly constant, or is the percentage increment roughly constant? The first is linear growth — steady, headcount- or account-driven. The second is compounding growth, typical of a product with network effects or active viral referral loops. Fit a linear model to compounding data and the forecast looks fine for a quarter or two, then the real curve pulls away from the straight line and capacity runs short exactly when it matters most.

A forecast is a range, not a point. The trend line's confidence band widens the further out you project — normal statistical behavior, not a flaw. The number that should drive a scaling decision is the upper bound of that band at your planning horizon, plus a deliberate headroom buffer on top, commonly twenty to thirty percent. Planning to the midpoint instead gives you roughly even odds of running out of capacity right when it counts.

A forecast number is only useful with enough lead time to act on it — a cloud quota increase, a reserved-capacity purchase, a database replica rollout all take real time to land. Get the forecasting discipline right, and the next question becomes whether your system can actually survive the load you just forecasted. That's where load testing comes in, and next lesson is about doing it in a way that actually predicts production behavior instead of misleading you.
